title: Fickle Fay Creep, Soapsuds and the manuscript Carew found
summary: Harrison Smith claimed Fickle Fay Creep as another tune; Carew traces it to Soapsuds, recovered through his nephew's records.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Now, when he did that, Harrison Smith right away claimed that that was a tune by one of his writers, you know. And he said it was the same tune as Just Alone the Echo, which was copyrighted, oh, three, four years before Jelly Roll recorded Fickle Faye Creep. So I went down to the library and I called out Just Alone the Echo. And boy, I couldn't make a head and a tail of the thing. So I don't know whether, yet today, I don't know whether there's any resemblance or not, but I do know that the, oh, that other one I mentioned, when you were talking about that other time, Soapsuds. Soapsuds, yes. It's the same tune. And he recorded that in St. Louis far ahead of when he went with the...
Did you find that? Did you get a...
Yeah, I have it. It's not too good, but it's there. It is the same as Fickle Faye Creep on the, I guess, on the Victor and on the library record.

Soapsuds by the, what, St. Louis? Levy Serenade. Levy Serenade, yeah. Okay. Okay record. I, well, as a matter of fact, I didn't have it. My nephew had that. See, I dropped out of all interest in music, you may say, just about the time Jelly Roll was coming into prominence. And I went to Georgetown at night for four years while I was working, and I was busy as I hoped to be, and I don't want to be again. And I dropped every other interest that I had, you know, just to get through Georgetown. And my nephew, in the meantime, he got interested in Ellington and some Morton and anything that came along that they played for him down at the stores, I guess. He acquired quite a few records. And so after he died, some years ago, they told me to take his records, so I took his records. And went through them casually, and I didn't pay any attention to much. And all of a sudden, I heard somebody, no, all of a sudden, I got a lot of music that his estate sent me after he died. They returned to me music. And in it was a manuscript, Soapsuds, General Morton. I said, Soapsuds, Soapsuds. He says, I believe there's a record around here for that name. And I went in there, it was Soapsuds, but by nobody in particular.
By Martin. Yeah, by Martin. That's what I said.
